title: Password reset and change
idea: A reset token is a one-time secret: the email carries it raw, the database keeps only its hash, and `resetForgottenPassword` matches that hash before expiry.

analogy.text: A one-time door code sent to your phone. The building stores only a scrambled copy, so staff cannot read it. The code expires and works once.
analogy.breaks: The code travels by email, so anyone with inbox access can use it.

points: `forgotPasswordRequest` saves a hash and expiry, then emails the raw token.
It replies the same whether or not the email exists.
`resetForgottenPassword` hashes the URL token, then finds an unexpired match.
`changeCurrentPassword` is secured: it reloads the user and checks the old password first.

hero.title: A reset link, start to finish

messages.label: POST /forgot-password
messages.note: The browser sends only an email address.

messages.label: save hash + expiry
messages.note: `generateTemporaryToken` makes the token. Only its hash and the expiry are stored.

messages.label: link with raw token
messages.note: The mail's link ends in the raw token. The API never stores that.

messages.label: 200, same reply
messages.note: The reply is identical whether or not the email has an account.

messages.label: POST /reset-password/:token
messages.note: The user opens the link and the page posts the new password. The token is in the URL.

messages.label: find sha256(token), unexpired
messages.note: The API hashes the URL token and looks for that hash with an expiry still ahead.

messages.label: user
messages.note: A match proves the caller holds the mailed token.

messages.label: new password, clear token
messages.note: `save` hashes the new password. The token fields and the refresh token are cleared.
Opening the same link again finds no user and gets `400`.

code.title: forgot and reset
code.caption: Two controllers on one router, with condensed earlier files. Press Run: link, expiry, new password, replay.

walk.text: A demo front-end URL and condensed earlier files: utils, a recording mail helper, a trimmed `User`.
Find the user. Only if one exists, store the token's hash and expiry.
Build the link from the configured front-end URL, not `host`, and mail the raw token.
The reply is the same for any email, known or not.
Hash the URL token and look for an unexpired match. No match is `400`.
Set the new password; the hook hashes it. Clear the token fields and end old sessions.
Request a link twice, expire it, then use a fresh one and replay it.

code.title: changeCurrentPassword
code.caption: A secured route, so a stand-in sets `req.user`. Press Run: a wrong old password, then the right one.

walk.text: Condensed: utils and a `User` with the pre-save hook and `isPasswordCorrect`.
Reload the user: `req.user` has no `password` field, so it cannot check one.
A wrong old password is `400`, not `401`: the session itself is fine.
Assign the new password and `save()`; the hook hashes it.
In the project `verifyJWT` guards this route. Here a stand-in loads `req.user` without the password.
Try a wrong old password, then the right one. Only the second changes the hash.

pitfalls: Reply identically for known and unknown emails, or the route reveals which accounts exist.
Query the hash and an unexpired expiry together, or expired links still work.
Reload the user in `changeCurrentPassword`: `req.user` has no password field.

quiz.why: The first reset clears the stored hash and expiry. The second finds no matching user and answers `400`.

takeaway: Reset links are credentials: random, hashed at rest, expiring and single-use.

starters: Why hash the reset token if it is already random?
Should changing a password log out my other devices?
